name: Priya Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm an apprentice lineworker for the regional power company, in the same valley I grew up in. My dad did this job for thirty years out of the same depot, so half the old guys knew me as a kid. Most days we're out on farm roads replacing poles, fixing lines the wind took down, and putting in new services for barns and houses. I'm still learning, still a bit clumsy with the hot sticks, but I love that I'm keeping the lights on for people I know.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's home life like around the job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live in my grandparents' old farmhouse, which they left to me, so there's no rent or mortgage. Erik, my partner, works on his family's dairy farm up the road. Between the house and what I've saved, about eight months of pay, I'm comfortable. I don't use any of the AI things, I don't even have the apps on my phone, and I don't miss them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Most of these things are more talk than anything. At church or at the depot I'd say the real work is still done by people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means life goes on the way it should. My dad's job is still my job, and the valley still needs us when a storm comes through. That's a comfort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep on with the apprenticeship and learn from the old hands while they're still here. I'd keep saving, maybe put a new roof on the farmhouse next summer. Nothing else would change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest thing you'd worry about in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The old guys retiring. Five of them go in the next three years, and that's a lot of knowledge walking out the door. I'd want to soak up as much as I can before they go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would any of this affect Erik?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Milk prices and the weather matter more to his family than computers. He'd laugh at the whole thing.

say: I'd say I'm **not surprised**; it was more talk than anything.
I'd tell people at church that **real work** is still done by people.
think: Privately, life goes on **the way it should**, with her dad's job now hers.
The valley still **needs lineworkers** when storms come.
do: Learn from the **old hands** before they retire.
Put a **new roof** on the farmhouse next summer.
S0.quote: My dad's job is still my job, and the valley still needs us when a storm comes through.
fieldNote: Her identity is tied to **family tradition** and her hometown.
Her worry is **knowledge loss** as veterans retire.
Her **inherited house** gives her real security.

steps.text: Shadow the five senior lineworkers before they retire
Put a new roof on the farmhouse next summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the big tech companies and city people who made this mess, and I'd say the trades will hold. At the depot I'd say keep your head down and learn your job well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm fine. Machines doing paperwork in the office doesn't change a pole in a farmer's field. Maybe the office at the depot shrinks, but that's not my side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the apprenticeship. If the company brings in new software, I'd learn the least I have to. I'd keep saving and maybe help my dad with his pension paperwork, because his office might go digital.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit annoyed at all the fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You blamed big tech. What would you want done about them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd vote for whoever says they'll keep jobs local and stop companies replacing people just to save money. I'm not one for protests, but I'd vote on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the valley would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Halvorsen at the depot desk, who answers when farmers call in outages. She knows everyone. If a computer answers instead, it wouldn't know to send us to the back gate at the Larsen place.

say: I'd blame **big tech** and city people for the mess.
I'd tell the depot to **learn your job well** and keep your head down.
think: Privately, **office paperwork** going digital doesn't change a pole in a field.
Her **side of the job** stays the same.
do: Learn the **least possible** of any new software.
Help her dad with **pension paperwork** going digital.
feel: She feels **mostly calm**, a bit annoyed by the fuss.
S1.quote: Machines doing paperwork in the office doesn't change a pole in a farmer's field.
fieldNote: She blames **big tech** and city people, typical of her views.
She'd act through her **vote**, not protest.
She values the **local knowledge** of office staff.

steps.text: Carry on with the apprenticeship at the valley depot
Vote for candidates who promise to keep jobs local

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's reckless, and the government should have stopped it. Families and towns like ours didn't ask for this. I'd say that at church and at the kitchen table, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it frightens me. The office stuff goes in 2028, and the robots come for the poles around 2031, when I'm thirty-two and finally good at the job. My dad's trade could end with me, and I'd hate that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on the house, keep every penny I can. I'd ask my dad and Erik's family what they think, because they've lived through hard times before. And I'd wait to see what the robots can really do, because I don't trust what they say on the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got the house and savings, so I won't go hungry, but I'd lie awake thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lie awake. What's the thought that keeps you up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That there won't be lineworkers for Erik's and my kids to become, if we have any. The valley's always had people who fix things. I don't want the valley to be a place where machines come from the city to fix us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the robots did arrive in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe work on Erik's farm, or help my dad with his workshop. I don't know. I'd figure it out, but it wouldn't be the same.

say: I'd call it **reckless** and say government should have stopped it.
I'd say it at **church** and home, not online.
think: Privately, robots by **2031** could end her dad's trade with her.
She'd be **thirty-two** and just getting good at the job.
do: Stop **spending on the house** and keep every penny.

**Wait** to see what robots can really do.
feel: She feels **anxious** and would lie awake at night.

fieldNote: Her fear is about **family legacy** as much as income.

steps.text: Cancel the farmhouse roof and keep the money saved

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is still too fast, but at least we'd see it coming. A trade is never wasted, so I'd tell young people to get their tickets anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gets me my ticket and some years of real work. But robots at 2034 still mean the same thing, just later. I'd be thirty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the apprenticeship, keep saving, maybe do the roof after all. I'd talk to my dad about his workshop as something to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, but quieter about it. I'd have time to get used to the idea, which isn't the same as liking it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's in your dad's workshop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He fixes farm machinery for neighbours, small engines, welding. It's not much money, but it's real work and it's local.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn anything new in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Welding, maybe, from my dad. Not computers.

I'd tell young people to get **trade tickets** anyway, because a trade is never wasted.

steps.text: Finish the apprenticeship and earn her ticket

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to protect the trades, if politicians actually do it. I'd want apprenticeships kept going, not cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels manageable. I'd be a proper lineworker for years before 2039, and maybe have kids by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the apprenticeship, do the roof, keep saving. I'd keep learning welding from my dad too, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, but mostly okay. It would sit in the back of my mind on long drives out to the farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your future kids about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a trade, work hard, and stay close to family. That's what got my dad through, and it'll get them through too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything good in this picture for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe less storm work at night, if robots take that. I wouldn't miss being up a pole at two in the morning in January.

I'd want **apprenticeships** kept going in the valley, not cut.

Put the **new roof** on the farmhouse and keep saving.
Keep learning **welding** from her dad, just in case.

S4.quote: I wouldn't miss being up a pole at two in the morning in January.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My dad's trade could end with me, and two years is no time at all. What would help is the government protecting apprenticeships and making companies keep local crews, and my family close.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about towns like ours. If the city decides how robots come in, places like the valley get forgotten.

headlineQuote: If the city decides how robots come in, places like the valley get forgotten.
portrait: Priya is a **27-year-old apprentice** at the regional power company depot in her home valley.
Her dad was a lineworker for **thirty years** out of the same depot.
She lives in her **grandparents' farmhouse**, has eight months saved, and never uses AI.
She blames **big tech** and city people, and would act through her vote and family.
She's calm when nothing changes but **anxious** when robots could arrive by 2031.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her **dad's trade** could end with her.
whatWouldHelp: Government protecting **apprenticeships** and local crews, and her **family** close.
